facility: Williams Geismar Olefins Plant, propylene fractionator reboiler rupture and fire, Geismar, Louisiana, June 13, 2013
source: U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, Williams Geismar Olefins Plant Reboiler Rupture and Fire, Case Study No. 2013-03-I-LA, October 2016 (public record)
question: On June 13, 2013, propylene fractionator Reboiler B at the Williams Geismar olefins plant ruptured about three minutes after an operations supervisor opened the hot quench water (about 187 F) to its tubes; it had been offline on standby for 16 months since maintenance in February 2012. Shell side process fluid: about 95% propane, balance mostly propylene and C4s. Reboiler B shell design: maximum allowable working pressure 300 psig, hydrostatic test 450 psig. Using the facility description, the schematic and the incident timeline, determine the failure mechanism and estimate with calculations the pressures that could be reached in the shell, explain why the reboiler was not protected from overpressure, and recommend the design, procedural and management changes that would prevent a recurrence.

data_register.quote: The Williams Geismar Olefins Plant, which employs approximately 110 people, is located in Geismar, Louisiana, approximately 20 miles southeast of Baton Rouge.
data_register.value: ~110 people; ~20 miles SE of Baton Rouge

data_register.quote: The Lummus Company designed and built the olefins plant in 1967, and Allied Chemical first operated it.
data_register.value: 1967 built by Lummus; Allied Chemical first operator

data_register.quote: In 1985, Union Texas Petroleum purchased the plant from Allied Chemical and sold it to Atlantic Richfield Company (ARCO) in 1998. Williams then purchased the facility in 1999.
data_register.value: 1985 Union Texas; 1998 ARCO; 1999 Williams; at incident jointly owned Williams Olefins LLC and SABIC, Williams sole operator

data_register.quote: The plant originally produced 600 million pounds of ethylene annually.
Over the years, the production capacity increased to 1.35 billion pounds of ethylene and 80 million pounds of propylene per year.

At the time of the incident, approximately 800 contractors worked at the Williams Geismar facility on an expansion project, with an end goal of increasing the production of ethylene to 1.95 billion pounds per year.
The reboiler that failed, EA-425B ("Reboiler B") was one of two reboilers (Reboiler A and Reboiler B) that supplied heat to the propylene fractionator
data_register.value: EA-425B Reboiler B; paired with Reboiler A serving propylene fractionator

data_register.quote: Reboiler B had been offline for 16 months while Reboiler A was in operation, but was clean and available for use when Reboiler A eventually fouled
where tube-side hot quench water vaporizes shell-side hydrocarbon process fluid, which is approximately 95% propane with the balance composed mostly of propylene and C4s
(This report refers to the propane mixture as "propane.")

data_register.item: Quench water inlet temperature to reboilers
data_register.quote: Quench water enters the propylene fractionator reboilers at approximately 185 °F
which enters the reboiler at a temperature of approximately 130 °F
In 2001, Williams installed valves on the shell-side and tube-side reboiler piping to allow for continuous operation with only one reboiler operating at a time.
The original propylene fractionator design had both reboilers continuously operating.
data_register.value: original: both continuously operating; modified: one operating, one isolated standby

data_register.quote: The heat exchangers are 24 feet 8 inches long end-to-end.
Each exchanger shell (the portion of the heat exchanger that holds the tube bundle) is approximately 18.5 feet long and over 5 feet in diameter.
The tubes are each ¾-inch in diameter, and each heat exchanger contains 3,020 tubes.
if one were to lay each tube from one heat exchanger end-to-end in a straight line, the tubes would span over 10.5 miles.
Depicted in Figure 3 as a two-pass heat exchanger for purposes of simplicity, the reboilers were six-pass heat exchangers.
The valves (gate valves) isolating the reboilers from the pressure relief valve at the top of the propylene fractionator were not part of the original design, and were installed in 2001.
data_register.value: gate valves isolate reboilers from column-top relief; added 2001

data_register.quote: The quench water that directly contacts the heated furnace effluent gases is part of a closed-loop water circulation system.

data_register.item: Quench water settler and fouling mechanism
data_register.quote: The quench water settler removes most of the tar material (Figure 2); however, some oily material remains in the quench water.
data_register.value: settler removes most tar; residual oily material causes fouling

data_register.quote: Over time, some of this material adheres to and builds up on the inside of process equipment such as heat exchanger tubes, resulting in a decrease in both heat transfer efficiency and quench water flow rate.
data_register.value: fouling = buildup reducing heat transfer and flow

data_register.quote: the quench water flow through the operating propylene fractionator reboiler (Reboiler A) had dropped gradually over the past day (Figure 5).
data_register.value: gradual drop over past day in Reboiler A quench flow

data_register.item: Initiating valve opening time and evidence
data_register.quote: The CSB determined that at 8:33 am, the operations supervisor likely opened the quench water valves on the offline reboiler, Reboiler B, as indicated by the rapid increase in quench water flow rate shown in Figure 6.
data_register.value: 8:33 am likely opened B tube-side quench valves

data_register.quote: Approximately three minutes later, Reboiler B exploded (Figure 7).
The force of the explosion launched a portion of the propylene fractionator reboiler piping into a pipe rack approximately 30 feet overhead (Figure 8).
Quench water flow rate rises when Reboiler B tube-side quench water valves are opened. Reboiler B ruptures approximately three minutes later.
A Williams operator working near the propylene fractionator at the time of the explosion died at the scene. The operations supervisor succumbed to severe burn injuries the next day.
167 personnel reported injuries. / Of the 167 workers who reported injuries, three were Williams employees and 164 were contractors.
The fire lasted approximately 3.5 hours, and Williams reported releasing over 30,000 pounds of flammable hydrocarbons during the incident.
The plant remained down for 18 months and restarted in January 2015.

rfi.issue: RFI-04 Standby initial condition - blocked-in liquid-full?
rfi.item: Reboiler B shell-side isolation state, liquid level/fill fraction, pressure and temperature before 8:33 am opening

alternatives.result: VB-20261028-A vented screening: heating 54.44C C3 feed at 19.19 bar with 903.9 kW duty LMTD 22.6C, pressure check 19.19 vs 21.7 bara limit utilisation 0.884 - stays at column pressure, no accumulation. Proves communicating shell boils safely instead of accumulating to 490-500 psig bubble or 6350-6760 psig hydraulic.

Relief sized for thermal-expansion + heat-input boiling keeps shell below 300 psig MAWP.

findings.evidence: 16 months B offline standby (p.7); 2001 shell gate valves allow one-online/one-offline vs original both-online (p.9, p.10 Fig.4); 13-Jun morning A flow drop past day (p.11 Fig.5); 8:33am supervisor likely opens B quench valves rapid rise Fig.6 (p.11); ~3 min later B explodes (p.11); piping launched ~30 ft overhead (p.11); 2 dead, 167 injured, fire ~3.5 hr >30000 lb released, 18 months down restart Jan 2015 (p.12); tube quench ~185 F vaporizes shell ~130 F ~95% propane balance propylene+C4s (p.9); relief at column top isolated by 2001 gates (p.10 Fig.4).
findings.limiting_value: Root cause: blocked-in liquid thermal (hydraulic) expansion + vapor-pressure rise of trapped propane heated toward 185-187 F quench with no relief (ASSUMPTION with reason: 187 F from brief, 185 F p.9; MAWP 300 psig/hydro 450 psig from brief, not in pp.6-13, verify U-1/nameplate)
findings.modification: Recognize as API 521 blocked-in heated-exchanger rupture, not column overpressure or reaction

findings.evidence: bubble_pressure tool 95/5 Propane/Propylene (ASSUMPTION with reason: p.9 ~95% propane balance mostly propylene+C4s, no assay, C4s omitted conservatively): 19.19 bar at 54.44C (130F p.9) rising to 34.96 bar (490 psig tool) at 85.0C (185F p.9) and 35.67 bar (500 psig tool) at 86.11C (187F ASSUMPTION brief). fluid_properties densities 440.6 kg/m3 at 54.44C/19.19 bar to 354.26/349.29 kg/m3 at 85/86.11C, vapour_frac 0.0 confirms all-liquid expansion demand. blocked_in_pressure from 19.19 bar/54.44C: beta 0.00824-0.00853/K, kappa 0.000601-0.000603/bar, stiffness 13.7-14.1 bar/K gives 439 bar (6350 psig tool) at 85C critical fill 0.794 and 467 bar (6760 psig tool) at 86.11C critical fill 0.782 if liquid-full; both exceed 300 psig MAWP and 450 psig hydro (ASSUMPTION brief). VB-20261028-A/B vented at same duty stays 19.19 bar util 0.884 vs 21.7 bara (=300 psig+14.7 ASSUMPTION).
findings.limiting_value: At quench temperature shell must reach >=490-500 psig even with vapor space, and 6350-6760 psig if liquid-full (tool psig gauge-correct) - exceeds 300 psig MAWP minimum, >20x if blocked-full
findings.modification: Size corrective relief for both regimes: vapor venting at bubble pressure + liquid thermal expansion; do not rely on column-top valve through closed gates

findings.evidence: Fig.4 + p.10: column-top relief protected fractionator + shells originally, but 2001 shell gates break path when closed. Original design (p.9) had no isolation need. No shell-side dedicated relief described in pp.6-13 (p.10). Opening tube-side valves while shell gates shut puts heat into dead volume (p.11).
